newsitem.title: USA: AMA Journal commentary backs state tobacco suits.
newsitem.headline: AMA Journal commentary backs state tobacco suits.

text.p: The states are better off seeking compensation from tobacco companies for health care costs rather than letting Congress broker a deal, according to a commentary published Tuesday in the Journal of the American Medical Association.

"If the Congress is actively involved in the negotiations toward a resolution, there is a greater likelihood that the tobacco companies will sculpt the agreement to suit their interests rather than the public interest," the commentary said.

"Historically, Congress has been more beholden to tobacco interests than to states, localities or public health concerns," added the essay, written by Stanton Glantz and colleagues at the Institute for Health Policy Studies of the University of California at San Francisco.
The attorneys general from 22 states have filed suits against the tobacco industry seeking to recover health care costs from smoking-related illnesses.

The commentary cited published reports from last summer that a congressionally sanctioned settlement was in the works under which tobacco companies would have paid billions of dollars to the states to settle all claims in exchange for immunity from lawsuits and a possible end of Food and Drug Administration jurisdiction over tobacco products.

"Though never finalized or released for public review, this proposal reportedly called for the payment by the tobacco companies of $6 billion in 1997, escalating to $10 billion per year in the fourth year and continuing for the next 11 years," the article said.

"Much of this one was to be paid to the states to reimburse them for Medicaid costs, and some was to be paid toward individual compensation for sick smokers and to fund tobacco control programs, primarily aimed at children," it added.

"The tobacco companies were to voluntarily adopt most of the proscriptions in the FDA (anti-smoking) regulations and the FDA would forfeit jurisdiction unless certain targets regarding the reduction in youth smoking were met," it said.
In exchange, the tobacco companies would have gained protection from most lawsuits, the article said.

The authors of the commentary said the settlement would have been a bad deal because it would have covered only a fraction of the annual medical and social costs of smoking in the United States, which the report placed at $100 billion.
The commentary said there should be a broad public discussion of any settlement.
